speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the past 60 years, Singapore has transformed from a developing economy with limited resources into a globally competitive powerhouse.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the heart of this success is our commitment to education.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: None of this progress would have been possible without the hard work and dedication of our teachers, educators, school staff and our Ministry of Education (MOE) headquarter staff.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we look ahead, we must continue to strengthen our education system by expanding pathways and adapting curriculum to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It must be equipped to support all learners, with different learning needs and speeds, at every stage of their life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the last two years, I spoke about ironman suits and multivitamins.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This year, I will be a bit more in.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I will focus my speech on what I call the 3 "INs": innovating the continuing education and training (CET) ecosystem; integrating support for the special education (SPED) sector; and inclusiveness in school admission.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is commendable that, today, we have a wide range of CET courses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, some programmes offered by different arms of the CET ecosystem may overlap and the proliferation of choice may leave many learners feeling overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This fragmentation can create inefficiencies and duplication in resources.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, there is a need to break down silos and identify gaps and overlaps.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, a strategic review of the CET ecosystem can support innovation for the next bound of the SkillsFuture movement and align it to the in-demand skills for the future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, a more cohesive CET ecosystem can lead to creating robust frameworks for credit recognition and transferability across institutions and industries, which can encourage a skills-first mindset, instead of the traditional emphasis on formal academic qualifications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Learners can have their acquired skills validated by a unified and credible authority, whether gained through formal education, short-term courses or on-the-job training.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This streamlined process of accreditation can be integrated with the MyCareersFuture portal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The review should also include an evaluation of school-industry partnership initiatives, such as the Institute of Technical Education's (ITE's) Work-Study Diplomas and the Teacher Work Attachment Plus, especially the outcomes for participants in terms of employability and career or wage progression, so as to further explore areas to improve and expand.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is commendable that MOE has made significant efforts to break down silos between mainstream schools and SPED schools, including increased opportunities for intermingling among children, as well as attachments, rotations and secondments for teachers, such as through the SPED Leadership Development Programme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, I believe that more can be done to ensure that SPED teachers, educators and staff are not overlooked in the policy decisions surrounding their well-being, protection and career progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I submit that the Ministry adopt a more integrated approach that brings together the full spectrum of support across MOE, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and our social service agencies (SSAs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This approach should also be extended to supporting SPED students.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The current SPED landscape is fragmented, which may limit the impact of these support systems on SPED students and their families.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There needs to be more "porosity" – to borrow an analogy from the Minister for Education – not only between mainstream schools and SPED schools, but also across education, healthcare, manpower and social services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The SPED sector is inherently diverse, comprising a wide range of physical, intellectual, emotional and behavioural needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A more concerted effort in bringing together professionals and experts across various fields to address these needs via tailored approaches can more holistically and seamlessly support SPED students throughout their education journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One area that warrants more attention is workforce transition support for SPED students.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I was deeply dismayed by a recent MSF report that showed a decline in positive attitudes and a rise in negative attitudes towards persons with disabilities in Singapore's workforce in 2023 compared to 2019.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Ministry can consider more school-to-work bridging programmes to connect SPED students to internship, apprenticeship and training-and-placement opportunities through stronger collaboration with industries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The third and final "In" is inclusiveness in school admission.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have come a long way in developing diverse and inclusive pathways for our students in mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While it is commendable that MOE and our schools have taken active steps to support students from lower-income families to participate in DSA, such as the Junior Sports Academy, we must acknowledge the inherent disparities that can exist within the DSA process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To conclude, our education system must aim to foster not only academic excellence, but also resilience, adaptability and holistic well-being.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: No other country has invested so heavily or innovated so rapidly in education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite MOE's efforts, many parents remain fixated on academic excellence or results, particularly excelling in exams, such as the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE), to secure spots in what they perceived as, "better" schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The greatest challenge lies in shifting mindsets to value diverse pathways to success and prioritise lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could removing the PSLE, a high-stake examination, and introducing a 10-year integrated programme from primary to secondary school level help to remove one hotspot or hotpoint, and maybe free time to also work on other important attributes and skills that support our future education model?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have brought up this topic of removing PSLE and through-train integrated programmes for years now.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But I think we need a deeper dive on this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is no longer a question of removing PSLE or not, through-train or not.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For adults, could every Singaporean gain access to formal skills development planning and coaching, not just those who are job-seeking?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could we also adopt achievable targets, like the 10,000-step health goal, to cultivate a habit of continuous learning?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, some multinational corporations (MNCs) I know set self-driven training goals, in terms of hours or programmes for their staff.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could this be explored and also scaled nationally?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A future-ready education must address technological disruptions, especially by artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Nations and companies are already leveraging AI to transform education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I seek MOE's clarification on two points.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the new literacy curriculum for learners in this age of rapid technological advancement?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, how can we ensure that our learners become originators of ideas, not just consumers or managers of AI outputs and risk undermining development of their own critical and creative thinking skills?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Barrier three – on students with special educational needs (SEN).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, let me talk about SEN students in mainstream schools and IHLs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond academics, they need life skills to navigate living and working, especially post-school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, while initiatives like SEN officers and learning support offices are very commendable and I really appreciate it, current support does seem to fall short.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, may I ask MOE what feedback has been received on the current support model for SEN students in mainstream schools and IHLs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is MOE's future plan in this space?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can stakeholders like the mainstream schools, IHLs, MOE's own special needs department, special education needs department and disability-focused SSAs and SPED schools even, improve knowledge sharing and best practices to strengthen support?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SPED students often need more time to master foundational skills for living, learning and working.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This leads to skills loss, reduced independence, and increased burdens on families and society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the Government commission a study to seriously address – study this "cliff-effect" and address the gaps thereof – and even adopt a top-up funding model for SEN adult learners, mirroring what was given before age 18?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, SPED leaders face overwhelming administrative workloads due to numerous policies and reporting requirements.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While I appreciate MOE's increased support over the years, and I really think they are very good people in MOE for this, I urge a review to limit policies and reports to only the essentials and also to streamline processes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could SPED schools tap on public-sector systems – the good ones, like Form.gov.sg —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Denise Phua, can you round up please?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: — GeBiz, or Demand Aggregated Vendor Lists to reduce their administrative burdens and improve efficiency?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: So, in conclusion, Madam, Singapore is at the forefront of creating a future-ready education system that empowers every individual.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: If any nation can turn this vision into reality, I believe, it is Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, I beg for your indulgence as I take this opportunity to make yet another call on the Government to implement a 10-year through-train programme in some schools where students can progress from primary levels to secondary levels without going through the PSLE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is an issue that I personally feel most passionate about.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I assure the Minister for Education that I continue to raise this not because I did not hear his concerns, but because I remain unconvinced that those concerns outweigh the merits of creating this additional educational path as an option for parents and students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister is concerned about how to cater to students with different learning abilities and needs in the 10-year through-train programme.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can be addressed in two ways: one, reducing class sizes to reduce the range of diverse learning profiles and abilities within each class; two, implementing Subject-Based Banding.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the class level, we can use these two ways to manage the range of learning profiles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But at the school level, students will still benefit from interacting with a wide range of students and learning to respect and deal with differences.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the end of streaming and introduction of Subject-Based Banding, schools are already catering to diverse learning profiles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister himself said this of Subject-Based Banding: "the positive outcomes in learning and social mixing give us confidence that this is the right thing to do." If we can do it with Subject-Based Banding, we can do it with a 10-year through-train programme.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister also made the point that PSLE is simply a means to help our children find a suitable learning environment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regular assessments within the school can also do this.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is well-known how stressful PSLE can be not just for students, but for parents as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of enjoying the time spent building bonds with their children, many parents, instead, spent the time nagging or disciplining their children to study harder and longer to do better in the PSLE, in their anxiety to ensure their children's future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such stress strains family relationships and adversely affects mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would not be surprising for anyone observing this to conclude that life is much better without children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A stressful education system can be a disincentive for parenthood.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it a coincidence that regions known to have the most stressful education systems like South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, also have the lowest fertility rates?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) also calls for class sizes to be reduced.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will provide greater opportunities for differentiated learning and allow teachers to personalise teaching and better support students with different learning profiles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With our total fertility rate falling steadily year after year, our student cohorts have been shrinking.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By maintaining teacher recruitment levels and keeping schools open even as student cohorts shrink, we can reduce class sizes, without compromising on the quality of teachers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By making PSLE optional, we may also be able to reduce academic competition and demand for tuition.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In such a scenario, MOE could re-employ teachers who have left the Education Service for the private tuition industry to reduce class sizes in schools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There will always be segments of the student population that is difficult for mainstream schools to cater to.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, if a small proportion of students require tuition, that is not worrisome, but if over half require tuition then that cannot be healthy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, examination preparation calls for memorising and repetition which are not skills that prepare our children well for a society that will soon be greatly changed by AI.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOE has identified the 21st Century Competencies (21CC), including values, social skills, critical thinking and so on, that are needed to prepare our students for the future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But without systemic changes, wanna bet what will be the outcome of a poll on parents which they consider more important, PSLE or 21CC?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is survival instinct to adapt our behaviour to that which brings rewards.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And right now, our education system rewards efforts in preparing for PSLE more than efforts in building 21CC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Simply exhorting parents to change their mindset is not going to cut it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a through-train programme, time freed from PSLE preparations can be channelled towards building such competencies and better prepare our students for the future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the Minister said, learning is a continuous journey, not just for 15 years, but for 50.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important to nurture the love of learning in our children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A high-stress, high-stakes examination like the PSLE at such a young age does not help to do that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, please take your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Before I begin, I would like to declare my position as a chief executive officer of an education institution.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, the majority of students' typical pattern of education after completing their "O" level is generally a binary one.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They either attend a junior college (JC) or a polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The key distinction between these two routes lies in the type of education they offer, with JCs focusing on academic study that leads to the "A" levels and, often, university after that; and polytechnics providing vocational and technical training through a diploma programme, with increasing pathways to university education too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This shift was aimed at streamlining admissions for increased focus on core subjects and specialised skills.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The L1R4 system applied to both polytechnic and JC admissions, but the subjects counted could differ.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There was a return to the L1R5 system for JC admission a few years later.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And presently, I believe that there are two systems, L1R4 for polytechnic admission and L1R5 for JC admission.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It might be good, in my humble opinion, to ensure parity between the two systems, especially with students opting for both JCs and polytechnics in their same application form as they make their initial choices.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As learning becomes more personalised and catered to students' interests and choices become more diverse, having one aggregate calculation system based on L1R4 would also narrow the JC-polytechnic perceived divide.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having the same point system for both also allows for recognition of different learning styles and interests, and alignment of entry points would also allow equality of access to higher education for both polytechnic and JC students to university in the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could I suggest that MOE review the post "O" level criteria for JCs to make it more aligned with that of polytechnics?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Still on JC, on 20 January 1969, National Junior College, the first JC, had its inaugural assembly with 572 students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It offered 40 subject combinations to students who could exercise wide choices in subject options to meet their interests and inclinations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Following that, several JCs opened their doors, with Hwa Chong Junior College the first Government-aided JC in Singapore, opening in 1974; and Catholic Junior College, starting in 1975 to combine pre-university courses offered by Catholic religious schools or orders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The JC system was created to optimise the use of teachers and laboratory facilities while providing more educational opportunities for pre-university students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It aimed at creating a challenging learning environment and helping students develop their talents academically and non-academically.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The merged JCs – Anderson Serangoon Junior College (ASRJC), Yishun Innova Junior College, Tampines Meridian Junior College and Jurong Pioneer Junior College (JPJC) – adopted names that combined the full names of the original colleges, with the name of the older JC coming first to reflect its history.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could MOE provide an update on the exercise to rejuvenate JCs across the island?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, continuous teacher training occurs through a system of different professional development opportunities provided by MOE, including paid professional development courses, staff training opportunities, conferences, mentorship programmes, attachments, leadership development tracks and study programmes for further education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are SkillsFuture courses focusing on specific areas of practice to further teachers' professional growth and I believe that all teachers in Singapore are entitled to 100 hours of paid professional development every year.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While a good preliminary foundation has been laid to ensure good training by the National Institute of Education (NIE), which also offers various degree courses and professional development programmes, I believe that continuing education is crucial to keep sharpening skillsets and keeping teachers relevant.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The focus on Research-Informed Practices also means that teachers need to update their practice with evidence-based pedagogies and strategies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, given the rapid developments in AI, technology and pedagogy and fast-evolving workplace landscape where skills must be practice-oriented, the emphasis must be on ensuring that our teachers improve the quality of their teaching through upskilling and continuous learning for teaching quality excellence throughout their careers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had previously made the point in Parliament via Parliamentary Questions relating to the importance of ensuring that our teachers have industry experience and exposure for their own professional growth that will, in turn, enhance the overall teaching and learning of our students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would now like to ask if MOE can share more on the various programmes that are in place for the professional development of our teachers and if there are any plans to enhance these programmes anytime soon?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Neurodiverse students, including those with conditions like attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), dyslexia, autism or other cognitive variations, learn in ways that are different from learning methods and strategies adopted by neurotypical students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Neurodiverse students' learning styles evolve from their strengths and challenges they face.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each neurodiverse student is different but there are common strategies and approaches can support neurodiverse learners in achieving success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include, focusing on their strengths, providing assistive technologies, allowing for visual and hands-on learning, and providing extended assessment-time alternative assessments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For students that need social support, there are also strategies for them to overcome anxiety and increase collaboration opportunities with their peers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Much progress has been made in MOE schools with learning support and I am heartened to say this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Internships are a big part of ITE and polytechnic education, giving students with critical industry exposure and experience to complement their learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are significant as they offer hands-on experience, helping these students apply classroom skills into real-world, real-life scenarios.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This practical exposure builds confidence and allows students to explore their interests and their strengths, helping with career and eventually, life choices.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Internships also augment soft skills such as communication, time management and self-directedness, which are essential ingredients for workplace success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These experiences help them thrive in professional environments and enhance social interactions with colleagues as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, internships promote independence by teaching students task management and handling responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A decade ago, Singapore launched SkillsFuture with the foresight that CET must be a cornerstone of our growth strategy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We recognised that industry transformation, technological advancements and global shifts would continuously reshape job roles and skill demands.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To future-proof our workforce, SkillsFuture was established to ensure that Singaporeans can adapt, thrive and seize new opportunities in an evolving economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many, both within and outside this House, question whether SkillsFuture is delivering on its full potential.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To further SkillsFuture's impact, we must shift our focus from making training accessible with ensuring that it directly contributes to career outcomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Swiss Federal Act on Continuing Education and Training establishes a structured framework to ensure high-quality, industry-relevant training.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It mandates strict accreditation standards of CET providers, ensuring that courses meet rigorous quality and workforce relevance criteria.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Crucially, CET in Switzerland counts towards formal qualifications that are integrated into hiring and career progression, ensuring that training translates into tangible employment outcomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst we appreciate that SkillsFuture funds thousands of courses, the current system does not distinguish adequately between high-quality programmes and those with limited workforce impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Employers and trainees struggle to identify which courses deliver strong job outcomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Funding is distributed relatively evenly across CET providers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Additionally, research funding currently available to Government-funded IHLs should be extended to qualified CET providers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will support the development of a new generation of world-class CET institutions to develop thought leadership in their respective domains of industry practice.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will enable professionals undergoing CET from these world-class institutions to remain at the forefront of emerging trends, new technologies and evolving global standards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By integrating the latest research into CET programmes, we can equip workers with cutting-edge expertise that strengthens Singapore's workforce effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Two, making CET a cumulative pathway to meaningful qualifications.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While individuals should have the flexibility to take standalone courses, CET should not be seen as short, unrelated training courses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Instead, it should be structured as a cumulative pathway to enable individuals to continuously learn and develop towards meaningful industry-valued credentials for specific jobs and professions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Switzerland's, again, work-study CET model provides a strong precedent, where employees undergo continuous training while remaining in the workforce, earning recognised qualifications that offers tangible employment and wage growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, this offers a structured learning pathway where individuals can train and work concurrently towards a degree qualification.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I encourage and strongly urge the Government to extend such structured CET pathways to other professionals, such as in finance, where many individuals already hold degrees but require systematic upgrading to deepen their expertise and stay competitive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By investing in a series of stackable, industry-relevant CET courses, finance professionals can enhance their skills in real-world while working.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These practice-based courses should be purposefully designed to count as credit toward postgraduate qualifications, such as advanced certifications, postgraduate diplomas and Master's degrees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Remarkably, the recognition that there could be such skilled worker shortages is not new.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As far back as the 1980s, observers noted that demographic changes could threaten the viability of economic progress on our island if human resource needs remain unmet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet today, we still see reports attesting that as many as four in five companies face workforce talent shortages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has, we are told, necessitated the continued stream of foreign migrant professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, many in this House face a seasonal pattern of appeals after examination results are announced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Young residents, as well as their parents, often come to our Meet-the-People Sessions in a desperate effort to appeal for entry for their children into a given tertiary institution or programme of study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Often, this applicant actually possess the necessary scores required for entry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, the limited number of spaces often mean that these local kids are unable to secure a spot, as spaces are filled by those who obtain grades better than their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These two problems, while seemingly unrelated, are actually not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Essentially, almost a half century after the matter of a potential skills shortage was first identified, our local schools seem still unable to fill the nation's tech worker shortfall, despite possessing secondary school students that are sufficiently talented and willing to pursue technically-oriented tertiary education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The proposal is not as pie in the sky as one might imagine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similar approach to tertiary education is used in other places, such as France, Germany and the state of California in the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In France, while entry into the private grande école system – and full disclosure, I teach at one such school – is indeed competitive and dependent on relative scores acquired in a national level exam, known as "concours", admission into the public university system is actually generally open to all who have passed the Baccalaureate, which is the equivalent of our local "A" levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: German universities also are more forgiving with entrance criteria with certain programmes, even practising free admission.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Essentially, all applicants that fulfill basic university and entrance qualifications are let in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Standards are maintained by introducing tougher courses in the earlier stages and having students voluntarily drop out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One instinctive argument against this proposal is that grades serve as a filter for whether the potential student is likely to make it into the desired course of study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is precisely why the proposal will retain minimum criteria for entry into programmes to ensure that those who embark on a certain course of study have a realistic chance of completion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The key difference is that students that would otherwise meet this threshold do not get rejected, simply because of their relative underperformance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another objection is that system may be brutal and if students were to drop out, they could incur a debt burden with no degree to show for it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, this also means that, at least in the earlier years, the system will require more funding to cater to a larger matriculating cohort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is precisely what the threshold criteria are for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the long run, this could even pay off economically, since employers would be able to hire workers that they need while reducing the cost of searching for talent from abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, experts say that skills learned in our tertiary institutions do not necessarily align well with their needs on the job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relevant skills are instead acquired with certification examinations, but the prerequisites or eligibility criteria for many of these certificates are actually incredibly accessible, often requiring only "O" or "N" level credits, and are not accompanied by a need for stellar grades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What we need to ensure, therefore, is a better alignment of training and the graduates that we churn out.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Wan Rizal, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Task education should be flexible, yet responsive to students' diverse interests and aspirations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Have they gained greater clarity in choosing their specialisation and have retention rates improved?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond exploration, how are polytechnics ensuring that such students receive adequate academic and career guidance?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As flexible work arrangements are implemented across schools, how will MOE ensure that there are sufficient teachers, allied educators and administrative staff to support this transition reasonably?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Ultimately, how will MOE ensure that technology is used effectively to support our teachers to reduce burnout and focus on nurturing students?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: SEN officers play a crucial role in supporting students with special needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry share if there is a target ideal number of SEN officers in mainstream schools and if so, what this is, and how it plans to continue enhancing the support and development of SEN officers?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Many mid-career Singaporeans want to upskill and stay competitive, but challenges, such as financial constraints and balancing work and family, remain.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Extending the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Training Allowance to part-time programmes is a welcome move.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Could MOE share how these programmes are selected and how they align with emerging industry demands?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: With a 24-month lifetime cap on training allowances, how will MOE support mid-career individuals needing further upskilling beyond this period?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: As we build a culture of continuous learning, what further steps will MOE take to encourage greater participation, especially among lower-income and vulnerable workers?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers lack access to training and development opportunities that are typically provided for traditional employees by employers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Given that freelancer-dominated sectors, such as arts and culture, media and design, rank among the world's fastest growing and rapidly transforming sectors, it is pressing and critical for the Government to boost training support for affected freelancers, such as arts educators, creative practitioners and media workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry share how freelancers can be supported by the new schemes, such as the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme and the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, for workers studying part-time?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider a top-up of SkillsFuture Credit (SFC) for freelancers who had utilised 50% or more of their existing SFC?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers would welcome such boosts in keeping skills relevant and livelihoods viable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Budget 2025 continues to reinforce SkillsFuture as a cornerstone of our nation's commitment to lifelong learning and preparing Singaporeans for the opportunities and challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my conversations with my Woodlands residents, I am heartened that more and more of my residents are becoming aware and increasingly open to going for skills training, even though there are still many sceptics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A big part of it is from their own experiences or experiences of people they know, who have not been able to find a job even after attending multiple skilling programmes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: You also need to have the skills to search, apply and interview for jobs, network, plan your next career move.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We also need to build up agency and resilience in our people while we create an enabling environment around removing biases and encouraging companies to hire people with potential and fill in the edges rather than look for a ready-made hire.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With the increased demand for skilling, how will MOE ensure that selected training providers have a good track record of positive employment outcomes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What more can be done to drive positive employment outcomes?

text: Schools usually hold trials to select only the best athletes to represent them at the national school games.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many students want to take up sports like badminton, basketball or football as their co-curricular activity (CCA) in school, only to be disappointed that they cannot get a place in the CCA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some are left with no choice but to join a CAA they have little interest in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many schools already do this, but some still do not.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To manage limited resources, schools could adjust the number of CCA places to match demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This way, schools can ensure that every student who wants to participate in sports at their skill level has the opportunity to do so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the other end of the spectrum, top performing student athletes who have the potential to represent Singapore at international competitions are often still required to train with their school's sports teams.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They should still be allowed to earn LEAPS 2.0 points while doing so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will discuss the sports aspect of this further in my cut at the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) COS debate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Progress has been made, especially with an inclusive dispute resolution framework set for finalisation in this quarter.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One key issue is the procurement process for instructors' services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, most schools only procure instructor services at the end of the school year for the next, resulting in a highly compressed and competitive bidding cycle.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, instructors face job insecurity as they receive little advance notice when their contracts are not renewed.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This leaves them with insufficient time to secure alternative employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, the lack of a structured handover process between outgoing and incoming instructors disrupts students' learning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Without proper transition planning, students experience interruptions in their training and development.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, instructors often bid for multiple contracts to maximise their chances of securing a role.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, some who receive multiple contracts later withdraw their overlapping commitments, leaving schools scrambling to find last-minute replacements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I urge MOE to work with NICA to review the current procurement system and introduce earlier notification of contract renewals or non-renewals, clear handover protocols and a more efficient —

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: This was from a survey conducted by Etiqa Insurance in 2023.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: Many young Singaporeans were also found to have relatively low confidence in investing and building emergency funds.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: In our fast-changing financial landscape, young Singaporeans have more to grapple with than previous generations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: We must support our youths in navigating these new realities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: To improve financial literacy education in Singapore, I would like to suggest a two-fold approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: First, I urge MOE to take a targeted and more in-depth approach to incorporating financial literacy education in the school curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: Financial literacy should be taught in a way that is both relevant to the students' lives and tailored to Singapore's unique financial ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: Financial literacy education must also constantly evolve to reflect new financial trends, such as Buy-Now-Pay-Later schemes and cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: Second, expand partnerships and funding for financial literacy programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: It is crucial to start financial literacy education as early as possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: A strong foundation means that Singaporeans are equipped with the financial know-how to manage money effectively, setting them up for life.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: That being said, I fully recognise the heavy workload that our teachers already shoulder.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: I am not suggesting that teachers bear this responsibility alone.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: We can tap on experienced external vendors to complement MOE's efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: MoneySense already promotes financial literacy through online resources and ad hoc talks, and then there are other organisations, such as The Volunteer Switchboard, who partners with corporates to conduct workshops for a select group of ITE students.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: By formalising partnerships with more of such organisations and expanding funding behind this, we can increase outreach, build up quality resources and bring in skilled trainers to complement existing efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: Imagine a future where every student graduates with the ability to manage their finances responsibly, a future where young Singaporeans feel confident and empowered to make sound financial decisions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: By taking action today, we equip our youths with the knowledge and skills to secure their financial future.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Excessive social media use amongst adolescents has been linked to an increased risk of anxiety and depression.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Addressing this issue requires a multifaceted approach involving families, schools and sustained interventions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One possible initiative is a disconnect to connect week, where students take a break from social media and engage in meaningful offline activities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While a short break may not change habits, it does encourage reflection on digital consumption and the wisdom to step away from online pressures.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Given these concerns, what steps will the MOE take to promote youth mental health in schools, particularly regarding excessive social media use?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Will it consider implementing a disconnect to connect week to support students' well-being?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: While our students excel in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) tests globally, we must consider whether our current assessment methods create opportunity cost at the expense of future critical skills, such as emotional intelligence, adaptability, creativity and critical thinking.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How are current assessment models aligned with the 21CC that MOE seeks to develop and nurture in our students?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Why does Singapore still have an examinations-based system for the "O" levels when the United Kingdom has already moved on from it in 1988 into the General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) model, which is more coursework-based in assessing students' learning and offers more flexibility in choosing pathways after?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Case in point, how are teachers marking composition and essay papers?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Do we still allocate or deduct marks for correct punctuation and spelling?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How can we shift the assessment criteria to focus more on the quality or originality of thought, creative expression and the ability to consider diverse perspectives over the accuracy of spelling and sentence structure?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: While MOE has been encouraging schools to approach learning differently with several curriculum revamps in recent years, are our assessment models reflecting these changes?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many students still face stress, anxiety and disengagement due to rigid assessment frameworks.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We still hear many stories of teachers who teach for tests or of parents who pressure teachers when they do not.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot fault parents for being "kiasu" when the assessment model remains the way it is.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Why not bring it forward to primary and secondary schools, too?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We must prioritise participation, engagement, articulation and other relational skills over technical correctness in the ways we assess children to best prepare them for their future.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: After all, AI can spell better and ensure accurate grammar better, too.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Oral examinations can take a higher weightage and allow students to choose topics of their own interest.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These can make up a larger portion of weightage, taking priority over paper examinations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These qualities are hard for parents to outsource to tuition centres to train for excellence.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, parents will need to engage their children at home and in the community in social interactions and conversations that build their perspectives and help them develop independence of thought.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: However, many healthy habits formed in school, if at all, do not carry over into adulthood.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Could MOE clarify if there are metrics to measure the success of physical health education?

text: If not, are there plans to strengthen the link between school physical health education and healthy adult lifestyles?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: This is important because we have seen that Singaporeans consistently rank one of the highest in stress levels around the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Besides families, schools play a part in addressing this issue.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I am concerned that our schools might take a "medical model" approach to mental health, in which students' mental health struggles are seen as problems to be fixed quickly rather than fostering lifelong stress management skills, with our varied personalities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng

text: What are the expected outcomes and what future plans are being considered to strengthen mental wellness education to achieve these outcomes?
